advaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita.english_rendering: This body, O Kaunteya, is called kṣetra (field): because it wastes, decays and perishes, or because the fruit of action is harvested in it as in a field. Whoever makes it an object of his knowing, from the soles of the feet to the crown, by native knowing or by instruction, and discerns it part by part, him the knowers of the two call kṣetrajña (knower of the field). Is field and knower known by this much alone? No; what more is to be known is now taught.
advaita.divergence_note: Śaṅkara (his 13.2) gives a fourfold etymology of kṣetra (kṣata-trāṇa, kṣaya, kṣaraṇa, field-like ripening of karma-phala) and defines the kṣetrajña purely as the one who objectifies the body, by svābhāvika or aupadeśika knowing. He closes by saying this naming is not yet sufficient knowledge, so the identity of this knower with the Lord is held back for the next verse. Unlike Śrīdhara and Madhusūdana he does not read 'vetti' as the I-and-mine of the bound self.

viśiṣṭādvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
viśiṣṭādvaita.english_rendering: This body, which a man speaks of in one breath with himself ('I am a god, I am a man, I am stout, I am lean'), is still other than the self who enjoys, and those who know the body truly call it the kṣetra (field) of that self's bhoga (experience); he who knows it, limb by limb and as a whole, as 'this I know' is, by being the knower, other than the known, and the knowers of the self call him kṣetrajña. We rightly say 'I am a man' only because the body exists solely as the self's viśeṣaṇa (mode), inseparable from it (apṛthak-siddhi), as cowness is from the cow. The knower's own form is not reached by the eye but by a mind refined in yoga; the deluded, standing near prakṛti (matter), see the knower in prakṛti's shape, as I shall say in 15.10.
viśiṣṭādvaita.divergence_note: Rāmānuja (his 13.1) builds the verse around sāmānādhikaraṇya (co-ordinate predication): 'I am a man' is true, but only because the body is an inseparable mode (viśeṣaṇa, apṛthak-siddhi) of the self, not because body and self are one. Self and body are each arthāntara (a distinct entity), knower and known, like a pot and its seer. This sets up his reading of 13.2, where field and knower are both modes of Bhagavān; no other school here uses the mode-grammar.

dvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
dvaita.english_rendering: Salutation to the giver of knowledge. In this chapter the Lord gathers into one the jñāna (knowledge), jñeya (the knowable), kṣetra (field) and puruṣa (person) taught earlier, and sets them out each distinguished from the others.
dvaita.divergence_note: THIN. The Madhva text supplied (his 13.2) is only a one-line chapter introduction; it glosses no word of this verse, not kṣetra, not kṣetrajña, not tad-vidaḥ. The one doctrinal signal is the emphasis on viveka (setting the four apart), which fits Dvaita but is not developed here. The rendering above translates the introduction itself, not a Dvaita reading of the verse, which the source does not supply.

śuddhādvaita.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
śuddhādvaita.english_rendering: This body, a transformation of the prakṛti already called not-self (anātman), is named kṣetra (field) because it is the dwelling of the puruṣa, as is the great cosmos, so is the small body. So long as the puruṣa does not know it as distinct he is only kṣetrin (holder of the field) and remains in saṃsāra (the round of birth and death); whoever knows the field apart, and himself as its seer, him the knowers call kṣetrajña (knower of the field). Even in saṃsāra there is some knowing of field and knower, but blurred into one; this separateness belongs to the one who knows himself as kṣetrajña, not to all.
śuddhādvaita.divergence_note: Vallabha (his 13.2) splits two statuses: kṣetrin, the mere occupant who is bound, and kṣetrajña, a title earned by distinct knowing. He rejects the extra opening verse ('prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva') that some editions add, calling it unused by all and the whole hexad an elaboration of chapter 7. Several phrases (sāmānādhikaraṇya, ātma-viśeṣaṇataika-svabhāvatayā tad-apṛthak-siddheḥ, the pot-and-seer example) are taken almost word for word from Rāmānuja; the supplied text also seems to swap para and apara prakṛti (field as para), which looks like a transmission error and is not built on here.

bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
bhakti.english_rendering: I promised to lift my devotees out of the sea of death and saṃsāra (rebirth), and that cannot happen without knowledge of the self; so now I teach the discrimination of prakṛti (nature) and puruṣa (person), the two natures, lower and higher, named in the seventh chapter. This body, the bhogāyatana (house of experience), is called kṣetra (field) because it is the ground where saṃsāra sprouts; he who 'knows' it, that is, takes it as 'I' and 'mine', is called kṣetrajña, because like a farmer he eats its harvest. So say the tad-vidaḥ, those who know how field and knower are told apart.
bhakti.divergence_note: Śrīdhara (his 13.2) places the whole chapter under the devotional promise of 12.7 ('I am their uplifter'): knowledge serves rescue. His decisive move is reading 'vetti' as abhimāna, 'I and mine', so the kṣetrajña of this verse is the bound jīva, a farmer eating the crop of karma. That is opposite to Vallabha, for whom kṣetrajña is the title of the one who has separated himself.

advaita-bhakti.reading_summary: (reading summary extraction pending; ENABLE_READING_SUMMARIES=true to generate)
advaita-bhakti.english_rendering: This body with its senses and inner organ, O Kaunteya, is called kṣetra (field), for in it the fruit of action ripens again and again like grain; whoever takes it as 'I' and 'mine' is called kṣetrajña (knower of the field), a farmer eating his own harvest. Mark the grammar: the field is named in the passive, as object, because it is inert, while 'kṣetrajña' stands with 'iti' and not as an object at all, because it is svaprakāśa (self-luminous); anyone may name the field, but only the vivekin (discerning) name its knower. This whole last hexad serves the meaning of the great sentence: that the kṣetrajña, one and changeless in every field, is not other than the non-dual paramātman (supreme self).
advaita-bhakti.divergence_note: Madhusūdana (his 13.2) opens with his own verse: let the yogī (meditator) see the attributeless light if he can; for us, let the blue radiance running on Kālindī's bank delight the eyes. He then frames chapters 13-18 as the vākyārtha (sentence-meaning, the jīva-brahman identity) after the tvam and tat hexads, takes Śrīdhara's farmer gloss, and adds a grammatical argument found nowhere else here: the knower is never put in the accusative because it can never be an object.

so_what_questions: When I say 'I'm exhausted' or 'I'm a surgeon', what exactly am I identifying with?
Can I look at my own body or health as something I know about, rather than as all that I am?
If my job or my body is the field, who is the one tending it, and does that one get tired too?
Is knowing yourself something everyone does by default, or a skill you have to earn?
Anyone can describe what I do; who is in a position to describe the one doing it?
Am I just living in my life, or do I actually know it?

everyday_applications.advaita: Before a hard day, a surgeon can run through her body from feet to head the way she reviews a chart: tight shoulders, short sleep, a dull headache. Each is something she knows, which is exactly what makes it field and not her. Śaṅkara adds that this inventory is only the first step; noticing that you are the one who sees is where the real work begins.
everyday_applications.viśiṣṭādvaita: When you say 'I'm sick' or 'I'm old now', you are not wrong, but you are using a shorthand. The body belongs to you the way a quality belongs to a thing: inseparable, yet not the thing itself. So care for it seriously, since it is yours, and still refuse to let its state decide what you are.
everyday_applications.dvaita: The commentary here only announces the chapter's method: take four things that were mixed together and set each out separately. A founder facing a messy crisis can start the same way, putting the product, the customer, the team and the money in separate columns before deciding anything. Nothing more specific can honestly be drawn from Madhva on this verse.
everyday_applications.śuddhādvaita: You can occupy a role for years without knowing it, like a tenant who never learns where the pipes run. Vallabha calls that being merely the holder of the field, and says that is exactly the stuck condition. The shift comes when you can describe your role clearly as something distinct from you, and see yourself as the one watching it.
everyday_applications.bhakti: Most of us 'know' our career or our house the way a farmer knows his plot: as mine, and as the place my rewards come from. Śrīdhara says that is exactly the stance that keeps us bound, and that any rescue from burnout has to start by seeing how 'my work, my status' is the soil the trouble grows in. Help comes, but it comes through that clarity, not around it.
everyday_applications.advaita-bhakti: Anyone at work can describe your output, your title, your health record, because those are objects. Only a discerning friend notices the one who is aware behind all of it, and that one never shows up on a performance review. Madhusūdana also keeps room for delight: the point of seeing clearly is not a cold abstraction but the freedom to enjoy what is beautiful in front of you.

primary_meaning: This body is called the field, Arjuna, and the one who knows it the knowers call the field-knower.
